Empirical Research Plan  
“Consequences of Winning a Narrow U.S. House Election, 1942–2008”

=================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) centered on the Democratic (or Republican) candidate’s vote‐margin relative to zero.

Why RDD?  
• Assignment rule is mechanical: the candidate (and thus party) with a vote margin > 0 wins.  
• Near the zero cutoff, districts are virtually identical on observables and unobservables; the winner is quasi-random.  
• The design naturally delivers a local average treatment effect (LATE) of “barely winning” versus “barely losing,” directly answering how close electoral victories translate into subsequent political/economic outcomes.  
• RDD avoids the parallel-trends requirement of DiD and the instrument search of IV; the discontinuity in treatment probability is built into the institution.

Extension: dynamic/event-study RDD (“difference-in-discontinuity”) to trace effects over multiple post-election cycles.

=================================================================
2. Treatment and Control Definition
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Unit of observation: Candidate-party × district × election year.

Running variable (R): Democratic vote share minus Republican vote share (or margin of the focal party minus opponent). Range: (-100, +100).  
Cutoff (c): R = 0.

Treatment indicator (T): 1 if R ≥ 0 (party wins seat), 0 otherwise.

Interpretation: Treated observations are districts where the focal party barely wins; control observations are districts where it barely loses.

Timing: Event date is election year t. Outcomes of interest measured in years t + k (k = 0, 1, 2 …, up to next few Congresses).

=================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff  
 Expected potential outcomes (political influence, spending, subsequent vote shares, etc.) are smooth in R absent treatment. Extremely plausible: whether a candidate wins by +0.2pp or loses by ‑0.2pp is driven by idiosyncratic factors (weather, ballot errors).  

A2. No precise manipulation / sorting around zero  
 Candidates cannot perfectly target a desired microscopic margin. U.S. House elections involve millions of voters; strategic manipulation at the precinct level cannot deterministically flip a margin of <1 pp.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) locally  
 Within the narrow bandwidth, each district’s outcome depends only on its own election result—not on adjacent districts whose margins are also close. Plausible given single-member districts.  

A4. Continuity in covariates at cutoff  
 Observable pre-t characteristics (e.g., prior turnout, socio-demographics) should not jump at R = 0. Can be empirically tested.

=================================================================
4. Main Threats and Remedies
-----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation of the running variable (fraud, recounts)  
 • Diagnostic: McCrary (2008) density test on R.  
 • Remedy: Exclude recount races if statutory recount thresholds correlate with margin; conduct robustness with and without such contests.

T2. Different candidate or party quality exactly at cutoff  
 Although continuous expectation of quality is assumed, unobserved quality might differ if higher-quality candidates tend also to win.  
 • Check balance in lagged covariates (campaign spending, prior office).  
 • Use donut RDD excluding |R| < 0.1 pp to remove margins with recounts or litigation.

T3. Post-treatment selection (incumbent retirement, redistricting)  
 Winning may change probability of running again, biasing long-run effects.  
 • Dynamic RDD/event study that re-centers each follow-up election on the *original* treatment.  
 • Estimate immediate (short-run) effects separately from medium-run outcomes conditional on seat continuation.

=================================================================
5. R Code Outline
-----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################################################
# 0.  Libraries
############################################################
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)      # RD estimation
library(fixest)        # high-dim FE regressions
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

############################################################
# 1.  Load and prepare data
############################################################
# Assume the CSV lives in the working directory
house <- read_csv("house_close_elections_1942_2008.csv")

# Key variables assumed in raw file:
#   year, district_id, dem_share, rep_share, winner_party,
#   outcome_next_win (1/0), fed_spending_pc, etc.

house <- house %>%
  mutate(running_var   = dem_share - rep_share,      # or margin for party of interest
         treat         = if_else(running_var >= 0, 1, 0),
         abs_margin    = abs(running_var),
         post_spend_ln = log1p(fed_spending_pc)      # example outcome
  ) %>%
  arrange(year, district_id)

############################################################
# 2.  Main RDD for outcome: probability of winning next election
############################################################
# Bandwidth selected via rdrobust’s IK selector
rd_out1 <- rdrobust(y = house$outcome_next_win,
                    x = house$running_var,
                    p = 1)                # linear local polynomial
summary(rd_out1)

############################################################
# 3.  Plot the RD
rdplot(house$outcome_next_win, house$running_var,
       binselect = "esmv",
       title = "RD plot: Incumbent advantage in next election")

############################################################
# 4.  Dynamic effect (event-study RDD for k = 0…3)
############################################################
for(k in 0:3){
  yvar <- paste0("vote_share_tplus",k)
  spec <- feols(as.formula(paste0(yvar, "~ treat | 0 | 0 | district_id")),
                data = filter(house, abs_margin <= 5))   # 5pp bandwidth
  print(summary(spec, se = "hc1"))
}

############################################################
# 5.  Robustness: alternative bandwidth & polynomial
############################################################
rd_out2 <- rdrobust(house$outcome_next_win, house$running_var,
                    p = 2, h = 3)   # quadratic, ±3 pp
summary(rd_out2)

# McCrary density test
rddensity(house$running_var)$test
```

=================================================================
6. Expected Results
-----------------------------------------------------------------
• Political persistence: Barely winning a House seat should raise the probability of winning the *next* election by roughly 25–35 percentage points, reflecting incumbency advantage (the canonical estimate is ≈30 pp).  
• Fiscal outcomes: Expect +3 % to +7 % higher per-capita federal outlays to the district during the subsequent congressional term, given the leverage of sitting members in securing appropriations.  
• Party-level advantages (committee assignments, leadership votes) likely accrue, but magnitudes are smaller and more diffuse.

=================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Sharp RDD)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff ……… 1  
C2: No manipulation of running variable ……………… 1  
C3: Covariate balance at cutoff …………………………… 1  
C4: Appropriate bandwidth / specification …………… 0.5 (choice can matter)  
C5: External validity beyond close elections ………… 0 (local estimate only)  

Total: 3.5 / 5.
